sentences.text: And here is our home: Earth.
The only place in the universe we know of that harbors life. 71 percent of its surface is covered with liquid water; that is why it looks blue from space.
Its strong magnetic field protects us from the solar wind, and the ozone layer filters ultraviolet rays.
The Moon's gravity, in turn, keeps Earth's axial tilt steady, so that the seasons stay regular.
Jupiter, king of the planets.
Its mass is two and a half times the total of all the other planets; 1,300 Earths fit inside it.
It has no surface; the colorful bands you see are giant cloud belts in an atmosphere of hydrogen and helium.
The Great Red Spot is a storm that has lasted at least 350 years and is larger than Earth.
This giant's day lasts only 10 hours, and more than 95 known moons orbit around it.
The Red Planet, Mars.
It takes its color from the rusted iron on its surface.
Its diameter is about half of Earth's, but it is home to the largest volcano in the Solar System: Olympus Mons, 22 kilometers high.
The Valles Marineris canyon, 4,000 kilometers long, is long enough to stretch from one end of the American continent to the other.
Billions of years ago there were rivers and lakes on its surface; today, robots are searching for traces of that water.
Our first stop is Mercury, the smallest planet and the closest to the Sun.
One trip around the Sun takes only 88 days.
Its atmosphere is so thin it might as well not exist; that is why the day side rises to 430 degrees while the night side drops to minus 180 degrees.
Its surface is covered with craters, just like the Moon.
Right now, Europe and Japan's joint spacecraft BepiColombo is on its way toward it.
The Moon is Earth's only natural satellite and the only other celestial body humans have set foot on.
Between 1969 and 1972, twelve astronauts walked on its surface on the Apollo missions.
It is 384,000 kilometers away and always shows us the same face, because its rotation is locked to its orbit.
Every year it moves about 4 centimeters farther from us.
Neptune, the farthest planet from the Sun.
It was discovered not with a telescope, but on paper: mathematicians studying the deviations in Uranus's orbit calculated its position, and in 1846 it was found right there.
Its winds exceed 2,100 kilometers per hour; they are the fastest winds in the Solar System.
One trip around the Sun takes 165 years.
Its large moon Triton orbits in the opposite direction; it is probably a captured Kuiper Belt object.
Our last stop is Pluto.
It was discovered in 1930 and was considered the ninth planet until 2006; it is now a dwarf planet.
Until New Horizons flew past it in 2015, it was nothing but a blurry dot.
The spacecraft found a giant heart shape, nitrogen glaciers, and mountains of water ice on its surface.
The surface temperature is minus 230 degrees.
Its moon Charon is so large that the two of them orbit together around a common center of mass.
Our Solar System tour ends here; have a good journey.
Saturn is, without a doubt, the most elegant planet in the Solar System.
Its rings are made mostly of water ice; their width reaches 280,000 kilometers, while their thickness is only about 10 meters in most places.
The planet itself is so light that if you put it in a big enough ocean, it would float.
At its north pole, a mysterious hexagonal storm rotates, each side as large as Earth.
Welcome to the Solar System tour.
Our journey begins at the center of everything, the Sun.
This star, 4. 5 billion years old, carries 99. 8 percent of the total mass of the system all by itself.
Its diameter is 1,400,000 kilometers; 109 Earths fit inside it side by side.
Its surface is 5,500 degrees, while its core is 15 million degrees.
The light you are seeing right now leaves here and reaches Earth in 8 minutes and 20 seconds.
Uranus, the planet lying on its side.
Its axis is tilted 98 degrees; that is, it all but rolls as it orbits the Sun.
Because of this, its poles experience 42 years of day and 42 years of night.
It looks blue-green because methane gas absorbs red light.
It is the first planet discovered with a telescope, by William Herschel in 1781, and only Voyager 2 saw it up close.
Venus is considered Earth's twin in size, but its conditions are a true hell.
Its thick carbon dioxide atmosphere raises the surface pressure to 92 times that of Earth and, through the greenhouse effect, drives the temperature up to 465 degrees.
It is hotter even than Mercury, which is closer to the Sun.
Its clouds are sulfuric acid.
Venus rotates in the opposite direction and very slowly: a day there is longer than a year.
